What Is AI Governance?

Explainerlowob research

By lowob · 30 July 2026 · Updated 16 November 2026 · 5-minute read · Strategy

AI governance is the set of roles, policies, records and controls through which an organisation decides how it uses AI, who is accountable for each use and how risks are found and managed. Three frameworks shape most programmes: NIST's voluntary AI Risk Management Framework, the ISO/IEC 42001 management system standard, and the EU AI Act. For a company of 20 to 500 people, governance starts with an inventory, named owners and a record of decisions, not a committee.

What AI governance means

Governance answers four questions for every AI use: is it allowed, who owns it, how is it checked, and what is recorded. Policy documents are the visible part. The working parts are an inventory of AI systems, an owner for each, a risk classification, approval rules and evidence that the rules were followed.

AI governance isAI governance is not
Named owners and decisions for each AI useA single ethics statement on the website
A risk-based inventory updated as tools changeA one-off procurement checklist
Evidence: approvals, logs, incidents, reviewsA tool that can be bought and switched on
Proportionate to the firm's size and exposureA copy of a large bank's framework

The three reference frameworks

NIST AI RMF. NIST describes the framework as guidance for voluntary use by organisations designing, developing, deploying or using AI. Its core has four functions: govern (culture, roles and policy), map (context and risks of each use), measure (assessment and tracking) and manage (prioritising and acting on risks). A companion Playbook suggests actions for each. The Generative AI Profile, NIST AI 600-1, applies the framework to generative systems.

ISO/IEC 42001. The standard "specifies the requirements and provides guidance for establishing, implementing, maintaining and continually improving" an AI management system. It is intended for any organisation providing or using AI-based products or services. Like ISO 27001 for information security, it can be certified by an accredited body: BSI announced Dutch accreditation in December 2024, and UKAS granted its first UK accreditation for 42001 certification in January 2026.

EU AI Act. The Act is law, not guidance, and classifies AI uses by risk. Prohibited practices and AI literacy duties applied from 2 February 2025, and general-purpose AI model rules from 2 August 2025. Article 50 transparency duties generally apply from 2 August 2026. The Digital Omnibus, in force since 27 July 2026, moved Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 and product-embedded high-risk systems to 2 August 2028.

FrameworkTypeBest used for
NIST AI RMF and AI 600-1Voluntary US guidanceStructuring risk thinking for each use
ISO/IEC 42001Certifiable international standardShowing customers a management system exists
EU AI ActBinding EU regulationLegal obligations by risk category

Governance is a record of decisions with owners, not a document that says decisions will be made.

How a mid-size company starts

Large-enterprise programmes do not scale down well. lowob's Gateway 0 asks for three decisions before any AI tool is bought, and the same logic gives a proportionate starting set.

StepWhat it producesFramework link
Inventory every AI use, including features inside existing softwareA list with owner, purpose and data touchedNIST map; ISO 42001 scope
Classify by exposureClient-facing, regulated or internal; check EU high-risk categoriesEU AI Act risk tiers
Set the autonomy level per useAnswer, draft, act with approval, act and report, act aloneNIST manage
Name approvers and a kill switch ownerA matrix of who approves whatEU AI Act Article 14 oversight
Record decisions and outcomesReason, owner, status and expected outcome for each changeISO 42001 documented information
Review quarterlyUpdated inventory and incident listNIST govern; ISO continual improvement

For many mid-size firms, customer due diligence will ask for this list before any regulator does. A buyer's security questionnaire asking how AI is governed is answered by the inventory and the decision record, which is why lowob argues governance should start on the commercial line.

lowob takeaways

  • Start with the inventory. Governance cannot cover AI uses nobody has listed.
  • Pick frameworks by purpose. NIST for structure, ISO 42001 for certification, the AI Act for legal duties.
  • Check the dates. EU high-risk obligations moved to December 2027 and August 2028.
  • Keep the evidence. Owners, approvals and outcomes recorded are what governance looks like to an auditor.

Common questions

What is AI governance?

The roles, policies, records and controls an organisation uses to decide how it uses AI, who is accountable for each use, and how risks are managed.

What is the difference between NIST AI RMF and ISO 42001?

The NIST AI RMF is voluntary guidance for managing AI risk. ISO/IEC 42001 is an international standard for an AI management system that an accredited body can certify.

When does the EU AI Act apply to high-risk AI?

After the Digital Omnibus, obligations for Annex III high-risk systems apply from 2 December 2027, and for AI embedded in regulated products from 2 August 2028.

Does a small company need AI governance?

Yes, in proportion. An inventory, a named owner per use, approval rules for client-facing output and a decision record cover most of what customers and regulators ask.
